chunks.heading: Chapter 14 460
chunks.content:
Chapter 14 460
Furthermore, introspection i d x _ 0 c 3 9 2 9 7 0 today is often API-driven. Modern orchestrators expose rich REST or gRPC interfaces
that external tools can query to collect system state, perform health checks, or trigger automated actions. For
example, an external alerting system might query the orchestrator's API to verify the number of healthy replicas of
a critical service and raise an alert if that number drops below a defined threshold.
Finally, while i d x _ 2 1 5 0 6 d 9 3 operators rely on dashboards and logs, many organizations have moved toward event-driven
introspection. Instead of polling, systems subscribe to cluster events, such as Pod creations, deletions, or status
changes, and react in real time. This event-based approach enables highly responsive automation and proactive
remediation strategies.
In summary, introspection is about making the invisible visible. It turns the orchestrator from a black box into a
glass box, where every important signal is captured, structured, and made accessible. Through metrics, logs, and
traces, we gain the ability not only to detect when something breaks but also to understand why.
A mature orchestration platform does not just keep the system running; it continuously tells you how and why it is
running the way it does.
The tasks of an orchestrator summary
In this section, we examined the many responsibilities an orchestrator assumes to keep a distributed,
containerized system running reliably and efficiently. We saw how it continuously reconciles the desired and
actual states of the cluster, automatically heals failed workloads, balances traffic, manages storage, and performs
zero-downtime deployments. We learned how orchestrators enforce security through encryption, RBAC, and
secrets management, and how they provide introspection through logs, metrics, and traces.
Together, these capabilities make it possible to operate complex applications at scale with a level of resilience and
automation that would be nearly impossible to achieve manually.
However, orchestration today goes beyond merely starting and stopping containers. It has become the backbone
for running entire applications, enforcing organizational policies, and empowering people, including developers,
operators, and platform engineers, to work together more effectively. Modern orchestrators are as much about
coordination as they are about automation. They unify technology, process, and human collaboration into a single
operational model that keeps the modern software ecosystem in harmony.
Overview of popular orchestrators
Now that we i d x _ b 8 1 8 8 e a 2 understand what an orchestrator does and why it is indispensable, it is time to look at the platforms
that make orchestration a reality. Over the past decade, a variety of orchestration engines have emerged, each

chunks.title: ultimatedockercontainerbookfourthedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 14 460
chunks.content:
taking a different approach to solving the challenges of running distributed systems at scale.
In the early days of container adoption, the focus was primarily on managing individual containers and ensuring
that they ran reliably across multiple hosts. But as systems grew more complex, orchestration evolved beyond
simply scheduling containers. It became about running entire applications, enforcing policies, and enabling teams
to collaborate effectively through automation.
Today, orchestration platforms do much more than keep containers alive. They provide a unified framework for
deployment, scaling, security, and observability — and increasingly, they serve as the foundation for modern
platform engineering. Among the many options that once competed for attention, a few clear leaders have
461 Introducing Container Orchestration
emerged. The following overview introduces these orchestrators, their key characteristics, and the scenarios in
which each one excels.
At the time of writing, Kubernetes is i d x _ c 3 7 b b 5 b 2 the undisputed leader in container orchestration. While several orchestration
engines were competing only a few years ago, the market has since consolidated. Today, almost every managed
container platform, whether on AWS, Azure, or Google Cloud, builds upon Kubernetes at its core.
Nevertheless, it is instructive to briefly look at how we arrived here.
Kubernetes – the de facto standard
Kubernetes i d x _ e 7 8 0 1 5 4 2 has long evolved from a promising open source project into i d x _ 5 d b 1 2 4 7 a the undisputed standard for container
orchestration. Originally developed at Google and later donated to i d x _ 9 0 5 9 e 3 6 1 the Cloud Native Computing Foundation
(CNCF), Kubernetes was designed to address one of the hardest problems in modern distributed computing: how
to deploy, scale, and manage applications reliably at massive scale.
At its core, Kubernetes is declarative in nature. Instead of issuing step-by-step instructions, you describe the
desired state of your application and its infrastructure using a set of resource definitions written in YAML or JSON.
Kubernetes then continuously reconciles this desired state with the actual state of the system. This reconciliation
loop is the heart of Kubernetes' control plane and the key to its self-healing and resilient behavior.
What truly sets Kubernetes apart is its extensible and modular architecture. Nearly every aspect of the platform,
from networking and storage to authentication and scheduling, can be customized or replaced. This extensibility is
powered by Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs), which allow operators and developers to introduce entirely
new resource types into the Kubernetes API. Many modern capabilities, such as service mesh sidecars or GitOps
controllers, build directly on this mechanism.

chunks.title: ultimatedockercontainerbookfourthedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 14 460
chunks.content:
The Kubernetes ecosystem has also matured significantly. Today, there is a rich landscape of tools and frameworks
that extend its functionality and simplify its day-to-day operations:
Helm introduces i d x _ 9 f 1 7 b 7 e 6 a package management model for Kubernetes, allowing complex applications to be
installed with a single command and parameterized through reusable templates.
Operators encode i d x _ c 7 a c a d 4 4 operational knowledge directly into software. They automate life cycle tasks such as
backups, upgrades, and scaling for specific applications or databases, all while adhering to Kubernetes'
declarative model.
GitOps tools such as i d x _ 8 f 8 9 4 9 f 8 Argo CD and Flux bring the principles of version control and continuous delivery to
cluster configuration. By storing manifests in a Git repository, GitOps ensures that any change to the
cluster is auditable, reviewable, and automatically applied.
Over the i d x _ b 3 7 9 b 8 0 3 past few years, Kubernetes has also become easier to i d x _ 1 0 e 6 0 6 2 8 consume. Managed services such as Amazon EKS,
Microsoft's AKS, and Google's GKE remove the operational overhead of maintaining a control plane and integrate
tightly with their respective cloud ecosystems. For local development or edge computing scenarios, lightweight
distributions such as K3s and MicroK8s make it possible to run fully compliant Kubernetes clusters on a laptop, a
Raspberry Pi device, or even in a single virtual machine.
Finally, Kubernetes continues to evolve with the introduction of the Gateway API, which modernizes the way
ingress and service-to-service communication are defined, and with deeper support for sidecar containers that
enable advanced networking, observability, and security patterns.
•
•
•

chunks.title: ultimatedockercontainerbookfourthedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 14 462
chunks.content:
Chapter 14 462
With its declarative design, rich ecosystem, and powerful extensibility, Kubernetes has not only become the default
platform for running containerized workloads but also the foundation upon which the modern cloud-native
landscape is built.
Kubernetes supports both Linux and Windows containers.
Docker Swarm – simplicity over features
Before i d x _ 7 7 0 5 0 b 7 8 Kubernetes i d x _ d 5 7 d 3 1 1 9 became the dominant force in container orchestration, Docker Swarm held a special place in
the hearts of many developers. Introduced by Docker as an integral part of the Docker Engine, Swarm brought the
power of clustering and orchestration to the masses. Its greatest strength has always been its simplicity.
With just a few straightforward commands, anyone could transform a group of Docker hosts into a functioning
cluster. Services could be defined declaratively through a familiar Docker Compose file, and with almost no
additional learning curve, a developer could deploy, scale, and update applications across multiple machines. The
same commands used for single-container workloads also worked in a Swarm environment, a philosophy perfectly
aligned with Docker's core promise of build, ship, and run anywhere.
Swarm was built with security and ease of use in mind. Out of the box, it enabled mTLS between nodes,
automatically rotating certificates and encrypting all inter-node communication. This focus on secure defaults
made Swarm remarkably approachable for smaller teams or those just beginning their journey into orchestration.
However, as the container ecosystem matured, users increasingly demanded finer-grained control, extensibility,
and integration with the broader cloud-native landscape. Kubernetes, with its rich API surface, extensibility
through CRDs, and thriving CNCF ecosystem, quickly overtook Swarm as the preferred platform for production
workloads.
Today, Docker Swarm continues to live on in maintenance mode, serving as a simple yet powerful orchestrator for
lightweight deployments, edge clusters, and educational environments. Its declarative syntax and minimal
operational overhead still make it an attractive choice for those who value ease of use over complex automation.
In retrospect, Swarm played an essential role in shaping the container era. It helped thousands of engineers grasp
the fundamental concepts of orchestration, including services, desired state reconciliation, load balancing, and
rolling updates, long before Kubernetes became the global standard. Even if its active development has slowed,
Docker Swarm remains an elegant example of how simplicity and usability can lower the barriers to entry in a
rapidly evolving technological landscape.
Docker Swarm supports both Linux and Windows containers.
Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS)

chunks.title: ultimatedockercontainerbookfourthedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 14 462
chunks.content:
As i d x _ c 9 c c 1 e 5 0 Kubernetes adoption spread i d x _ c 8 8 9 4 1 a c rapidly across the industry, maintaining and securing a production-grade cluster
became a significant operational challenge. Recognizing this, Amazon introduced the Elastic Kubernetes Service
(EKS) to provide a fully managed Kubernetes control plane that integrates natively with the rest of the AWS
ecosystem.
EKS removes the burden of managing cluster internals such as control plane components, etcd, or API server
availability. Instead, AWS operates and scales these parts automatically, ensuring a highly available, multi-
Availability Zone (AZ) control plane with built-in security hardening and automated updates. This allows teams
463 Introducing Container Orchestration
to focus on what matters most—namely, deploying and running their workloads, without worrying about the
cluster's underlying mechanics.
One of the greatest strengths of EKS is its deep integration with AWS infrastructure and security services. It ties
directly i d x _ b 5 c b 7 5 4 a into AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), enabling fine-grained, identity-based permissions for
Pods through the IRSA feature. Network integration with Amazon VPC allows each Pod to receive its own IP
address via the VPC CNI plugin, providing native networking capabilities and seamless interoperability with
existing AWS services.
EKS also supports multiple compute options for running workloads. Besides traditional EC2-based worker nodes,
AWS i d x _ 6 e 8 d b c c 3 offers Fargate integration for fully serverless container execution, where Pods are scheduled onto abstracted
compute instances that scale automatically and bill by the second. This combination of managed control plane and
serverless data plane provides the best of both worlds: operational simplicity and fine-grained control when
needed.
In recent years, AWS has made EKS even more approachable by simplifying cluster provisioning through eksctl, an
official command-line utility that abstracts away much of the complexity of i d x _ e 1 f d d 5 4 3 initial setup. At the same time, EKS
Anywhere extends Kubernetes management beyond AWS to on-premises environments, allowing organizations to
run consistent clusters across hybrid or edge setups with a single operational model.
EKS represents i d x _ 1 5 4 5 7 f 7 b Amazon's commitment to open standards and cloud-native interoperability. Rather than building a
proprietary orchestrator, AWS embraced Kubernetes as the industry standard and surrounded it with the
reliability, scalability, and enterprise-grade security that the AWS platform is known for.
Today, EKS is one of the most widely used managed Kubernetes services in the world, chosen by organizations that
want to harness the full power of Kubernetes without having to manage its operational complexity themselves.

chunks.title: ultimatedockercontainerbookfourthedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 14 462
chunks.content:
Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)
Microsoft's Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) is another major managed Kubernetes offering and one i d x _ 5 6 2 3 4 1 5 1 of i d x _ 4 2 e 2 e 7 d 3 the
earliest large-scale cloud implementations of Kubernetes. Like Amazon EKS, AKS takes away much of the
operational overhead associated with running a production-grade cluster, such as managing the control plane,
patching nodes, or upgrading cluster components.
At its heart, AKS delivers a fully managed control plane with automatic scaling and self-healing capabilities. The
worker nodes, which can run on virtual machines or spot instances, are orchestrated by Azure and can be upgraded
or replaced with minimal disruption. This allows teams to focus entirely on deploying and scaling their
applications rather than managing the underlying infrastructure.
One of the key strengths of AKS lies in its deep integration with the broader Azure ecosystem. It natively connects
i d x _ 4 3 b 1 d d 4 6 with Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure Active Directory) for unified authentication and RBAC, enabling
organizations to reuse existing enterprise identity structures and governance models. AKS also integrates
seamlessly with Azure Monitor, Log Analytics, and Application Insights, providing out-of-the-box observability
and troubleshooting capabilities across the full application stack.
Networking in AKS is equally flexible and powerful. With Azure CNI, Pods can be assigned IP addresses directly
within the i d x _ 4 a 5 c 4 7 7 4 Azure Virtual Network (VNet), allowing fine-grained network policies and secure communication
between Kubernetes workloads and other Azure services. Advanced i d x _ e 5 0 a 2 b 6 3 users can also enable Azure Private Link,
isolating the Kubernetes API server from the public internet to strengthen cluster security.

chunks.title: ultimatedockercontainerbookfourthedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 14 464
chunks.content:
Chapter 14 464
AKS has evolved into i d x _ e c 0 f 8 4 d 7 a mature and feature-rich platform that supports the full Kubernetes ecosystem, including
Helm, Operators, and GitOps tools such as Flux or Argo CD. In addition, Microsoft provides Azure Arc, an extension
that allows AKS clusters to be managed alongside on-premises or multi-cloud deployments through a single
control plane.
Another notable capability is automatic node provisioning and scaling. AKS supports virtual nodes, powered i d x _ 7 a 0 2 a 4 0 2 by
Azure Container Instances (ACI), enabling serverless container execution that automatically adjusts capacity
based on workload demands. This elasticity combines the cost benefits of serverless execution with the governance
and consistency of Kubernetes.
Through AKS, Microsoft has fully embraced the open, cloud-native model, making Kubernetes a first-class citizen
in the Azure ecosystem. It empowers teams to run highly available, secure, and compliant workloads in the cloud,
on-premises, or at the edge, all managed through familiar Kubernetes abstractions.
AKS demonstrates how Kubernetes can be deeply integrated into a cloud platform while still preserving its open
source foundation. With a focus on developer experience, enterprise-grade security, and hybrid flexibility, AKS has
become one of the most polished and approachable Kubernetes offerings available today.
Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE)
If Kubernetes i d x _ d f 7 8 d d 3 3 is the beating heart of the modern i d x _ 6 e 7 1 1 6 b 6 container ecosystem, then Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) is
the environment where it was first perfected. Developed and operated by the very engineers who created
Kubernetes, GKE is widely regarded as the most mature and feature-complete managed Kubernetes service
available today.
From the beginning, Google designed GKE to demonstrate Kubernetes' full potential at planetary scale. The
platform provides a fully managed control plane, distributed across multiple zones for high availability and
resilience. Cluster upgrades, patching, and backups are handled automatically, allowing engineers to deploy and
operate workloads without being distracted by infrastructure maintenance.
One of GKE's defining characteristics is its tight integration with Google Cloud's networking and security stack.
Every cluster benefits from Google's global SDN, ensuring low-latency connectivity and strong isolation between
workloads. Features such as Workload Identity allow Pods to authenticate securely against Google Cloud APIs
without the need for long-lived credentials, while Binary Authorization and Shielded GKE Nodes enforce supply
chain security and protect against image tampering or unauthorized workloads.
Beyond these core features, GKE has long been a pioneer in Kubernetes innovation. It was the first managed service

chunks.title: ultimatedockercontainerbookfourthedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 14 464
chunks.content:
to offer auto-repairing and auto-upgrading node pools, as well as horizontal and vertical Pod autoscaling that
dynamically adjust resource allocation based on demand. GKE also supports Autopilot mode, a fully serverless
option in which Google manages both the control plane and the worker nodes. In Autopilot, users simply define
workloads and policies, and Google ensures that the necessary compute, scaling, and maintenance happen
transparently in the background.
GKE's support for multi-cluster and hybrid deployments is another major strength. With Anthos, organizations
can manage Kubernetes clusters running on Google Cloud, on-premises, or i d x _ 0 0 1 0 b 7 1 5 even on other cloud providers, all
through a unified management plane and consistent policy enforcement. This flexibility allows enterprises to
adopt a true hybrid or multi-cloud strategy without losing the operational consistency that Kubernetes provides.
465 Introducing Container Orchestration
The GKE ecosystem also integrates deeply with Google's data and AI services. Many teams use GKE to orchestrate
machine learning workflows with Kubeflow, run data pipelines, or serve AI i d x _ b 5 f b b 2 9 4 models at scale using GPUs and TPUs.
This demonstrates how orchestration has expanded beyond traditional web workloads to power the next
generation of intelligent, data-driven applications.
In summary, GKE remains the benchmark for managed Kubernetes services. It combines operational excellence,
cutting-edge innovation, and deep cloud integration. For many organizations, GKE represents the purest
realization of the Kubernetes vision: a self-healing, scalable, secure, and declarative platform capable of running
workloads anywhere, from cloud to edge, with the reliability of Google's global infrastructure behind it.
HashiCorp Nomad — a lightweight alternative
While Kubernetes i d x _ c c 6 6 c 7 e 2 dominates the world of container orchestration, not every use case demands its complexity or
huge set of features. Some teams seek a more lightweight, pragmatic solution, one that combines operational
simplicity with flexibility. HashiCorp Nomad fills i d x _ 5 8 4 4 7 7 b 3 exactly this niche.
Nomad was designed with a singular focus on simplicity and performance. Unlike Kubernetes, which was built
exclusively around containers, Nomad can orchestrate heterogeneous workloads, ranging from Docker containers
and Java applications to raw binaries, virtual machines, and even batch or scheduled jobs. This makes it especially
appealing for organizations running a mix of legacy and modern workloads that need a single, unified scheduler
without the overhead of maintaining multiple orchestration platforms.
At its core, Nomad follows a monolithic yet elegant architecture. A single lightweight binary can be deployed on

chunks.title: ultimatedockercontainerbookfourthedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 14 464
chunks.content:
every node in a cluster, handling both client and server responsibilities. This design drastically reduces operational
friction and makes Nomad extremely easy to install and upgrade; a simple Nomad agent command can bootstrap
an entire cluster.
Despite its minimalist i d x _ 8 c 8 f 5 a 9 b design, Nomad provides a powerful and resilient scheduler capable of handling thousands
of nodes and millions of allocations. Its multi-region federation feature enables global-scale deployments,
allowing workloads to be distributed intelligently across data centers or cloud regions. The system automatically
performs load balancing, reschedules failed jobs, and optimizes placement based on user-defined constraints such
as CPU, memory, or affinity rules.
Nomad's simplicity i d x _ 8 c b 2 6 c a 1 is complemented by tight integration with other tools from the HashiCorp ecosystem. Consul
can be used for service discovery and networking, while Vault manages secrets and identity. Together, they form a
secure, composable, and highly portable orchestration environment that works seamlessly across cloud and on-
premises infrastructure.
Although Nomad does not aim to compete feature-for-feature with Kubernetes, it deliberately avoids unnecessary
complexity. It has no requirement for CRDs, ingress controllers, or a sprawling control plane. Instead, Nomad
appeals to teams who value a minimal operational footprint and prefer a straightforward scheduler that "just
works."
In recent years, Nomad has also gained popularity in edge computing and hybrid cloud scenarios, where resource
efficiency and reliability matter more than deep ecosystem integrations. Its small binary size, fast startup time, and
low memory consumption make it ideal for constrained environments.
In essence, Nomad embodies a different philosophy of orchestration, one centered around practical simplicity,
flexibility, and robustness. For many organizations, especially those orchestrating diverse workloads or operating

chunks.title: ultimatedockercontainerbookfourthedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 14 466
chunks.content:
Chapter 14 466
outside large-scale Kubernetes ecosystems, HashiCorp Nomad provides an elegant, lightweight alternative that
balances capability with clarity.
Historical note – Mesos and classic ECS
Before Kubernetes became the unifying standard for container orchestration, the landscape was far more diverse.
Several systems competed for dominance, each exploring different approaches to scheduling and managing
distributed i d x _ 1 9 a c 1 b 5 2 workloads. Among these, Apache Mesos and Amazon's Elastic Container Service (ECS) stood i d x _ d 8 4 b b 2 3 3 out as
early pioneers that helped shape what orchestration would eventually become.
Apache Mesos emerged i d x _ c 5 a 3 2 8 8 c from research at the University of California, Berkeley, as a general-purpose cluster
manager capable of running both containerized and i d x _ 2 7 8 b 2 0 2 a non-containerized workloads. It introduced many
foundational ideas that later appeared in Kubernetes, including resource isolation, fine-grained scheduling, and
multi-framework support. Mesos could orchestrate everything from long-running services to Hadoop and Spark
clusters, making it extremely flexible. Its companion framework, Marathon, provided a higher-level abstraction for
running containerized applications and served as one of the first production-ready orchestrators in the Docker era.
However, Mesos' flexibility came at the cost of complexity and operational overhead. Running and maintaining a
Mesos cluster required considerable expertise, and as container adoption surged, developers increasingly favored
systems that offered simpler, opinionated workflows. Over time, Kubernetes' declarative model and thriving open
source community rendered Mesos less relevant, and most organizations gradually migrated away from it.
Around the same time, Amazon ECS offered a fully managed orchestration solution tightly integrated with the
AWS ecosystem. ECS simplified container scheduling and scaling for developers already familiar with AWS
infrastructure, providing a convenient on-ramp to containerized workloads without requiring external
dependencies. ECS predated EKS and served as a bridge for many organizations transitioning from traditional EC2
deployments to container-native architectures.
While ECS i d x _ a 4 7 f 8 8 6 b continues to exist and evolve, now supporting both EC2 and Fargate execution models, its proprietary
design and limited portability led many users to favor the more open and extensible EKS once Kubernetes became
mainstream.
Both Mesos i d x _ 0 c d 4 9 e c 8 and ECS deserve recognition for laying the groundwork on which modern orchestration systems are
built. They proved the importance of automation, resource scheduling, and service health management long before
Kubernetes popularized these ideas across the broader industry.

chunks.title: ultimatedockercontainerbookfourthedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 14 466
chunks.content:
Today, these early orchestrators stand as milestones in the evolution of distributed computing, serving as vital
stepping stones that paved the way for the standardization, openness, and ecosystem maturity that define
container orchestration as we know it.
When to use which orchestrator
With so i d x _ 4 b f b 2 8 4 e many orchestration platforms available, the natural question arises: which one should I use? The honest
answer is that it depends, specifically on the size of your organization, your operational maturity, and your long-
term goals.
Kubernetes is the default choice for most modern environments. It offers the richest ecosystem, the broadest
support across all major cloud providers, and a highly extensible architecture that can grow with your needs. If
467 Introducing Container Orchestration
your goal is to build a scalable, cloud-agnostic platform with strong community support and open standards,
Kubernetes is the clear winner.
Amazon EKS, AKS, and GKE are ideal if you want the power of Kubernetes without the burden of operating your
own control plane. Choose between them based on your existing cloud footprint; stay within the provider you
already use, as each integrates deeply with its surrounding ecosystem.
Docker Swarm still has a place in smaller setups or learning environments. If you need to deploy a handful of
services quickly, prefer a minimal operational footprint, or are working on a project that values simplicity over
advanced automation, Swarm can still be an excellent fit.
HashiCorp Nomad shines in scenarios where workloads are diverse and not limited to containers alone. It's
especially well-suited for hybrid environments, edge computing, or cases where operational simplicity and
portability matter more than ecosystem size.
Finally, historical orchestrators such as Mesos and classic ECS are now of mostly educational interest. They remind
us how far orchestration technology has come, but in practice, nearly all new i d x _ 3 9 8 6 d 9 8 0 deployments today are built on
Kubernetes or Nomad.
In short, consider the following:
For enterprise-scale systems, choose Kubernetes (managed or self-hosted)
For simplicity and ease of use, use Docker Swarm
For mixed workloads and low overhead, pick Nomad
For cloud-native convenience, prefer EKS, AKS, or GKE, depending on your provider
Each orchestrator serves a purpose. The key is to align the tool with your team's skills, operational goals, and the
complexity you are truly ready to manage.
Emerging orchestration trends
Container i d x _ 0 5 9 1 9 d d 9 orchestration has come a long way since the early days of Docker Swarm and Apache Mesos. Today,
Kubernetes has become the standard foundation for running distributed workloads, both in the cloud and on-
premises. Yet, the story of orchestration is still evolving. The boundaries between containers, virtual machines, and

chunks.title: ultimatedockercontainerbookfourthedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 14 466
chunks.content:
serverless workloads are becoming increasingly blurred, and new trends are emerging that redefine what
orchestration really means in modern computing.
Serverless containers
One of the most i d x _ 4 6 3 9 5 4 8 b significant developments in recent years is the convergence of container orchestration and
serverless computing. Traditional orchestration platforms are excellent at keeping long-running services available,
but many modern workloads are event-driven and short-lived. Serverless container offerings such as AWS Fargate,
Google Cloud Run, and Azure Container Apps combine the flexibility of containers with the elasticity of serverless
execution.
In these models, you still package your application as a container, but you no longer manage any nodes or clusters.
The underlying orchestration layer scales the container instances automatically based on demand, even down to
zero when idle. This shift enables organizations to focus purely on application logic rather than infrastructure,
while still benefiting from the consistency and portability of containers.

GitOps and declarative management
Another i d x _ 2 4 8 d 4 9 c 3 strong trend is the adoption i d x _ 5 6 e 0 0 7 2 6 of GitOps principles in orchestration. GitOps extends Kubernetes' declarative
model by introducing version control and continuous delivery practices to the infrastructure itself. With Git as the
single source of truth, every change to a cluster, whether it's a deployment, a configuration update, or a policy
change, is represented as a commit.
Tools such i d x _ d e c 4 d f 1 9 as Argo CD and Flux watch i d x _ 8 1 2 2 0 d 5 a these repositories and automatically reconcile the running system with the
declared state. This approach improves auditability, enables full rollback through Git history, and brings
infrastructure management closer to standard software engineering workflows. In many organizations, GitOps has
become the operational backbone of modern platform engineering.
Multi-cluster and edge orchestration
As applications i d x _ 6 2 b c 3 c c d increasingly span multiple regions and environments, orchestration must extend beyond a single
cluster. Multi-cluster orchestration allows workloads to be deployed, observed, and managed consistently across
hybrid or multi-cloud setups. Kubernetes federation and tools such i d x _ 2 4 4 8 b 4 e e as KubeFed, Anthos, and Azure Arc provide i d x _ 4 f 1 8 3 e 1 9
this layer of control, enabling unified policy i d x _ d 6 b 8 4 0 c c enforcement and workload placement across many clusters.
At the same time, edge computing is reshaping orchestration at the opposite end of the spectrum. Lightweight
Kubernetes distributions i d x _ 3 b 3 c 8 b 6 0 such i d x _ 9 8 2 f 5 6 d 9 as K3s, MicroK8s, and k0s make it feasible to run fully i d x _ 4 2 1 a e f 6 5 functional clusters on small
form-factor devices or embedded systems. These edge clusters can synchronize with centralized control planes,
enabling workloads to run close to the data they process, which is a crucial capability for IoT and low-latency
applications.
AI-driven scheduling and optimization
With the i d x _ 9 f 4 3 f 2 3 3 rise of data-intensive and machine learning workloads, orchestration systems are being extended to
support AI-assisted scheduling and resource optimization. New components, such as Kubernetes' Kueue or i d x _ 6 5 d 5 e 4 3 7 the
Cluster Autoscaler with predictive scaling, leverage telemetry data and machine learning models to anticipate
demand and optimize placement.
These intelligent schedulers can make dynamic decisions about where and when to run workloads based on
performance, cost, or energy efficiency. Over time, this will lead to more autonomous orchestration systems that
continuously learn and adapt to real-world usage patterns without requiring manual tuning.
Security and policy as code
As i d x _ f 5 0 d 7 8 6 3 orchestration becomes the foundation of enterprise infrastructure, security and compliance have become first-

chunks.title: ultimatedockercontainerbookfourthedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 14 468
chunks.content:
class citizens. Modern i d x _ 0 3 d b c 4 4 e clusters increasingly integrate policy-as-code frameworks such as Open Policy Agent (OPA)
and Kyverno, allowing i d x _ e 2 3 8 d 2 3 0 teams to enforce governance and security rules declaratively.
These policies i d x _ 5 a 2 f 5 1 4 7 can validate configurations, restrict network access, or ensure images originate from trusted
registries, all before a workload is deployed. Combined with initiatives such i d x _ 1 c 7 f f e e 1 as Software Bills of Materials
(SBOMs) and the Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts (SLSA) framework, orchestration i d x _ 8 3 4 a e 7 9 9 platforms are
now playing a key role in maintaining end-to-end software supply chain integrity.
469 Introducing Container Orchestration
Abstracted platforms and developer experience
Finally, as i d x _ 1 4 f 4 b 7 b 4 orchestration technology matures, there is a growing movement to hide its complexity behind i d x _ 1 4 5 0 5 a d 4 higher-
level i d x _ 3 c b 2 2 6 1 f developer platforms. Internal developer portals such as Backstage, Port, or Humanitec offer i d x _ 1 5 8 d 3 5 4 7 user-friendly
interfaces that allow engineers to deploy and monitor applications without having to interact directly with
Kubernetes.
This evolution marks a shift from infrastructure-centric to developer-centric orchestration. The focus is no longer
solely on managing clusters, but on delivering a friction-free developer experience where provisioning
environments, deploying services, and applying policies are self-service, secure, and automated.
This evolution aligns closely with the principles i d x _ f b 4 c 3 a b 3 of platform engineering, where orchestration becomes a behind-
the-scenes capability that powers internal developer platforms.
Summary
In this chapter, we learned why container orchestrators have become indispensable for running distributed
applications reliably at scale. We discovered how orchestrators continuously reconcile a system's desired state with
its actual state, ensuring that workloads remain healthy, responsive, and correctly distributed across the available
nodes.
We explored the key responsibilities of an orchestrator, ranging from scheduling and service discovery to scaling,
self-healing, and secure configuration management. We also reviewed the most prominent orchestration
platforms and their typical use cases. Kubernetes clearly stands out as the dominant standard, supported by all
major cloud providers and surrounded by a thriving ecosystem of tools and extensions. Lighter alternatives such as
Docker Swarm and HashiCorp Nomad, however, still serve well in scenarios where simplicity or mixed workloads
matter more than ecosystem depth.
Finally, we looked at the emerging trends that are shaping the future of orchestration. Serverless containers,

chunks.content:
GitOps automation, policy as code, AI-driven scheduling, and internal developer platforms all point toward an era
where orchestration becomes increasingly autonomous, secure, and developer-friendly.
In the next chapter, we will take a closer look at Kubernetes, the orchestrator that has redefined how modern
systems are deployed and operated. We will explore its architecture, its core building blocks, and how it enables
developers and operators to run highly available, self-healing, and scalable applications both in the cloud and on-
premises.

What advantages do managed Kubernetes services such as EKS, AKS, and GKE provide compared to self-
managed clusters?
How does the adoption of GitOps and policy as code improve the management and security of container
orchestration environments?
What are the most important emerging trends shaping the future of container orchestration?
Answers
Here are some exemplary answers to the chapter's questions:
Container orchestrators automate the deployment, scaling, networking, and healing of containers across
clusters of machines. They ensure that applications remain available and consistent even when
individual nodes or containers fail.
The desired state defines how the system should look, for example, how many replicas of a service should
be running. The orchestrator continuously compares this desired state with the actual state and
reconciles any differences automatically.
Kubernetes became the standard because of its open governance under the CNCF, declarative model, rich
extensibility through APIs and CRDs, and deep ecosystem integration across all major cloud providers.

Introducing Kubernetes
In this chapter, you will learn how Kubernetes—the industry-standard container orchestrator—automates the
deployment, scaling, and management of containerized applications. You will explore its architecture and core
building blocks, set up a local cluster using Docker Desktop, minikube, or kind, and learn how to deploy and
observe workloads in action. Finally, you will discover key ecosystem tools such as GitOps, Helm 3, and Kustomize,
which bring automation, consistency, and simplicity to modern Kubernetes operations.
In the previous chapter, Chapter 14, Introducing Container Orchestration, we explored how orchestrators simplify the
complex task of running distributed, containerized applications at scale. We learned how they reconcile the
desired and actual state of a system, perform scheduling, service discovery, and scaling, and even apply self-healing
and security mechanisms automatically. By now, you should have a solid understanding of what an orchestrator
does and why it has become indispensable for modern software systems.
It is now time to look i d x _ e 5 0 3 f 0 2 5 more closely at the orchestrator that has redefined the industry standard: Kubernetes.
Originally developed at Google and later donated i d x _ 1 7 d 9 f 7 b 9 to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF),
Kubernetes is today the most widely adopted orchestration platform. It embodies many of the concepts we
discussed earlier—declarative management, self-healing, and desired-state reconciliation—and extends them
with an exceptionally rich ecosystem and extensible architecture.
In this chapter, we will explore how Kubernetes works under the hood. We will start by looking at its high-level
architecture and understanding the roles of the control plane and the worker nodes. You will learn about the key
components of the system—such as the API Server, Controller Manager, Scheduler, and the etcd data store—and
how they collaborate to maintain the cluster's desired state.
We will then move to the practical side and learn how to run Kubernetes locally using lightweight options such as
Docker Desktop, minikube, or kind (Kubernetes in Docker). These tools make it easy to experiment with
Kubernetes on your own machine before deploying workloads to a cloud provider. You will set up your first cluster,
deploy simple workloads, and observe how Kubernetes manages and exposes them through its built-in
abstractions.
From there, we will gradually introduce the fundamental building blocks of Kubernetes: Pods, ReplicaSets,
Deployments, and Services. Each of these plays a distinct role in defining how applications are packaged,
replicated, updated, and made accessible within the cluster. Understanding these concepts is essential for

chunks.title: ultimatedockercontainerbookfourthedition
chunks.heading: Chapter 20, Real-World Containerization Patterns
chunks.content:
mastering Kubernetes, as nearly every higher-level construct builds on top of them.
Finally, we will look beyond the basics and explore popular tools and practices that have grown around Kubernetes
—specifically GitOps, Helm 3, and Kustomize. These tools bring automation, configuration management, and
reproducibility to the next level. They enable teams to treat their cluster configurations and deployments as
version-controlled artifacts, making it easier to scale and manage complex systems reliably.
After reading and practicing the exercises in this chapter, you will be able to do the following:
Explain the high-level architecture of Kubernetes, including the roles of control-plane and worker nodes
Describe what a Kubernetes Pod is and how it differs from a standalone container
Define and deploy ReplicaSets, Deployments, and Services to manage and expose your applications
Run a local Kubernetes cluster using Docker Desktop, minikube, or kind
Deploy a sample application to your cluster and inspect how Kubernetes maintains its desired state
Understand how modern tools such as GitOps, Helm 3, and Kustomize simplify deployment automation
and configuration management
With this knowledge, you will not only be able to deploy applications into Kubernetes but also truly understand
what happens behind the scenes—how the system maintains health, scales workloads, and enforces the
declarative model that makes cloud-native operations possible.
Let's begin our deep dive into Kubernetes—the orchestrator that has become the backbone of today's cloud-native
world.
Technical requirements
To follow along with the examples in this chapter, you need a working Docker environment and one or more local
Kubernetes options installed. All examples can be executed on macOS, Windows, or Linux. You will primarily work
with the command line and use kubectl, the official Kubernetes command-line interface.
Make sure that you have the following software installed and running on your system:
Docker Desktop (latest version): Includes a fully functional, single-node Kubernetes cluster i d x _ 4 1 1 9 f 8 2 7 that can be
enabled through its settings panel. It also installs the kubectl CLI automatically.
kubectl (if not installed via Docker Desktop): The command-line tool used to interact with i d x _ 8 f 9 4 8 7 6 5 Kubernetes
clusters. You can verify its installation with the following:
$ kubectl version --client
minikube (optional): A lightweight tool that runs a single-node Kubernetes cluster locally. It is ideal for
testing and experimenting. Installation instructions can be i d x _ 1 9 5 c 0 4 a 9 found at https://minikube.sigs.k8s.io/.
kind (optional): An alternative i d x _ 7 0 8 5 8 b 0 9 tool for running Kubernetes clusters using Docker containers as nodes. It
is widely used for testing and continuous integration (CI) environments. Installation instructions are

Understanding Kubernetes architecture
A Kubernetes cluster i d x _ 0 1 9 0 8 0 4 f consists of a set of servers. These servers can be VMs or i d x _ a 8 7 8 e 0 f e physical servers. The latter is also
i d x _ 0 e f e c 4 3 5 called bare metal. Each member of the cluster can have one of two roles. It is either a Kubernetes master or a
(worker) node. The former is used to manage the cluster, while the latter will run an application workload. I have
put worker in parentheses since, in Kubernetes parlance, you only talk about a node when you're talking about a
server that runs application workloads. But in Docker and Swarm parlance, the equivalent is a worker node. I think
that the notion of a worker node better describes the role of the server than a simple node.
In a cluster, you have a small and odd number of masters and as many worker nodes as needed. Small clusters
might only have a few worker nodes, while more realistic clusters might have dozens or even hundreds of worker
nodes. Technically, there is no limit to how many worker nodes a cluster can have, though you might experience a
significant slowdown in some management operations when dealing with thousands of nodes.
On the Kubernetes worker nodes, we run Pods. This is a new concept not present in Docker or Docker Swarm. A
Pod is the atomic unit of execution on a Kubernetes cluster. In many cases, a Pod i d x _ 5 2 f 6 2 6 e 5 contains a single container, but a
Pod can consist of many containers running co-located. We will describe Pods in much more detail later in this
section.
All members of the cluster need to be connected by a physical network, the so-called underlay network. Kubernetes
defines one flat network for the whole cluster. Kubernetes does not provide any networking implementation out of
the box. Instead, it relies on plugins from third parties.
Kubernetes just defines i d x _ 0 2 8 f b c 2 9 the Container Network Interface (CNI) and leaves the implementation to others. The
CNI is pretty simple. It states that each Pod running in the cluster must be able to reach any other Pod also running
in the cluster without i d x _ 2 4 6 0 4 6 8 e any Network Address Translation (NAT) happening in between. The same must be true
between cluster nodes and Pods—that is, applications or daemons running directly on a cluster node must be able

Currently, Kubernetes masters only run on Linux. The most popular Linux distributions, such as RHEL, CentOS,
and Ubuntu, are supported. On this Linux machine, we have at least the following four Kubernetes services
running:
API server: This is the gateway to Kubernetes. All requests to list, create, modify, or delete any resources
in i d x _ f 0 e 3 1 4 7 0 the cluster must go through this service. It exposes a i d x _ 5 f b e c 7 9 e REST interface that tools such as kubectl can use
to manage the cluster and applications in the cluster.
Controller: The controller, or i d x _ 7 4 4 d 9 e c d more precisely the controller manager, is a control loop that observes i d x _ 2 2 b 2 9 9 0 2 the
state of the cluster through the API server and makes changes, attempting to move the current or
effective state toward the desired state if they differ.
Scheduler: The scheduler i d x _ a 9 e 2 d f 6 d is a service that tries its best to schedule Pods on worker i d x _ 0 c 0 b e c b d nodes while
considering various boundary conditions, such as resource requirements, policies, quality of service

We need at least one master, but to achieve high availability, we need three or more master nodes.
Kubernetes masters never run i d x _ b 6 1 5 3 9 5 7 application workloads. Their sole purpose is to manage the cluster. Kubernetes
masters build a Raft consensus group. The Raft protocol i d x _ 0 d 8 3 3 5 d 4 is a standard protocol used in situations where a group of
members needs to make decisions. It is used in many well-known software products such as MongoDB, Consul
(HashiCorp), and Kubernetes.

How the control plane collaborates
Although the control-plane components are separate processes, they cooperate through a shared
control loop centered around the API server and etcd. Every component interacts with the cluster
exclusively through the API server. When a user or automation tool submits a resource definition
—such as a Pod or Deployment—the API server stores this desired state in etcd. Controllers
continuously watch the API server for changes and attempt to reconcile the current state with the
desired state. The scheduler then assigns newly created Pods to suitable worker nodes. Finally,
the kubelet on each node observes the assigned workload and instructs the container runtime to
start or stop containers accordingly. Through this continuous feedback loop, Kubernetes
automatically drives the system toward the declared desired state.

Introduction to local Kubernetes
Before deploying applications to a i d x _ b 3 4 3 c c a 8 production-grade Kubernetes cluster, it is essential to first experiment in a safe
and local environment. Fortunately, Kubernetes can be run directly on your laptop or workstation using
lightweight distributions that behave just like a real cluster. These local setups are ideal for learning, testing, and
rapid development because they provide the same APIs, configuration model, and command-line tools as their
cloud-based counterparts.
In this section, we will i d x _ d c 5 2 a d b 5 explore the most i d x _ 6 6 a e 2 e 0 1 common options for running Kubernetes locally: Docker Desktop,
minikube, and kind. Each of them has its own strengths, and together they i d x _ d 8 3 8 a 8 3 7 cover nearly every learning and
development scenario you might encounter.
Docker Desktop with Kubernetes
If you are using Docker Desktop on macOS, Windows, or Linux, you already have everything you need to run a fully
functional single-node Kubernetes cluster. Docker Desktop ships with Kubernetes built in; it just needs to be
enabled once through the graphical settings.
To enable Kubernetes i d x _ 8 8 3 b f 3 1 1 in Docker Desktop, follow these i d x _ a 6 7 1 7 d a 8 steps:
Open the Docker Desktop application.
Go to Settings | Kubernetes.
Check Enable Kubernetes and optionally select Show system containers (advanced).
